captions: Everything so far has been lossless.
Every bit recovered,
perfectly,
down to the last one.
That is what you need for a text
file or a bank statement.
But think about a photograph,
or a song,
or a movie.
Do you truly need every bit back,
exactly?
Or just something your eyes and ears cannot
tell apart from the original?
The moment you are willing to accept a
little error,
a whole new door opens — lossy compression.
And with it comes a fundamental trade-off.
Look at this curve.
Along the bottom is distortion — how much
error you will tolerate.
Up the side is the rate — how
many bits you must spend.
At the top left,
you insist on near-perfect fidelity,
and you pay for it with a big,
heavy file.
Slide down and to the right,
and you accept more blur,
more noise — and the file shrinks dramatically.
This curve is not a guess or a
rule of thumb.
Its exact shape is fixed by a branch
of the theory that Shannon founded,
called rate-distortion theory.
For a given amount of acceptable error,
it names the smallest possible number of bits.
And this is the theory living inside your
daily life.
JPEG for images.
MP3 for music.
Every video codec that streams to your screen.
They all do the same clever thing.

They spend precious bits only where your
perception
can actually notice — the sharp edges,
the loud notes — and they quietly throw
away the fine detail you were never going
to miss.
Lossless compression removes what is redundant.
Lossy compression removes what is imperceptible.
Both are just information theory,
deciding what truly matters.
